items.example_en: I have a headache.
items.note: Body part plus 疼: the part is the topic and 疼 the comment.

items.example_en: Give me your hand.
items.note: 手臂 is arm. 把 fronts the object before the verb.

items.example_en: My legs ache after running.
items.note: 脚 is the foot. 完 marks the finished action.

items.example_en: My back has hurt since yesterday.
items.note: 从 ... 开始 means starting from.

items.example_en: I have a stomach ache.
items.note: 胃 is the organ; 肚子 is the everyday word.

items.example_en: My throat hurts, it's hard to talk.
I'm hungry, let's eat something.
items.note: An adjective, so no 是: 我很饿, never 我是饿.

items.example_en: Are you thirsty? There's water in the fridge.
I'm hot, can you open the window?
items.note: One word covers both you and the weather: 我很热 and 天气很热.

items.example_en: I'm sleepy, I'm off to bed.
items.note: 累 is physically tired, 困 is sleepy.

items.example_en: I need to rest for a bit.
items.note: 一下 after a verb means briefly, just a little.

items.example: 不好意思，洗手间在哪儿？
items.example_en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
items.note: The polite term in any public place.

items.example: 从早上开始我就不舒服。
items.example_en: I've felt unwell since this morning.
items.note: 舒服 is comfortable; 不舒服 covers everything from unwell to uneasy.

items.example_en: He's had a fever for two days.
items.note: Duration goes after the verb, with 了 at the end for ongoing.

items.example_en: I cough badly at night.
items.note: 得 introduces how the action is done.

items.english: to catch a cold, a cold
items.example_en: I have a bit of a cold.
items.note: Both the verb and the noun. 有点 means somewhat, with a negative flavour.

items.example_en: It hurts here when you press.
items.note: 的时候 marks when, and follows the clause.

items.example_en: How long have you had this pain?
items.note: 多 plus adjective asks about degree: 多久, 多远, 多大.

items.example_en: Register first, then wait to be called.
items.note: The first step at any Chinese hospital, before seeing a doctor.

items.example_en: I'd like to book tomorrow's outpatient clinic.

items.example: 这是您的处方，去药房拿药。
items.example_en: Here's your prescription, collect the medicine at the pharmacy.
items.note: 药方 is also used.

items.example_en: Take this medicine after meals.
items.note: Chinese EATS medicine, it does not take it.

items.example_en: You need to rest for three days.
items.note: Duration follows the verb: 休息三天.

items.example: 昨天晚上我们去了急诊。
items.example_en: We went to A and E last night.
items.note: The emergency number in mainland China is 120 for an ambulance.

items.example_en: I exercise three times a week.
items.note: Frequency goes before the verb: 一周三次.

items.example_en: I run along the river.
items.note: Verb-object compound: 跑了半个小时步 splits it.

items.example_en: I got a gym membership.
items.note: 办卡 means to get a membership card.

items.example_en: She works out every morning.
items.note: Slightly more formal than 做运动.

items.example_en: You look really healthy!
items.note: 身体 covers both body and general health.

items.example_en: My whole body aches today.
items.note: 酸 literally means sour, and is the standard word for muscle ache.

items.example_en: I didn't sleep well last night.
items.note: The negative of 得 complements uses 没: 没睡好.

items.example_en: Take a rest, you need it.
items.note: 吧 softens a suggestion into a friendly nudge.

items.example_en: Work stress leaves me exhausted.
items.note: 让 plus person plus adjective: makes someone feel something.

items.example_en: I want to properly relax at the weekend.
items.note: 好好 before a verb means properly, thoroughly.

items.example_en: You have to look after yourself in winter.
items.note: 好 as a result complement: look after well.

items.example_en: Take care on your way!
items.note: A warm parting word, especially for a longer separation.
